Allow more flexible glob matchers for runic js/ts modules
body:
### Describe the problem

When you want to write runic code outside `.svelte` files you require to use the `.svelte.js` or `.svelte.ts` extension. This is fine and benefits compile times. 

The issue with this is that it can easily conflict with other libraries/frameworks that also utilize files extensions, in my case: Vitest.
Sveltekit by default through the `npm create svelte` CLI adds the following matchers:
```js
export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [sveltekit()],
	test: {
		include: ['src/**/*.{test,spec}.{js,ts}']
	}
});
```
This means when you require runic code inside test files you need to first rename your test file to `.test.svelte.ts` and then add the matcher to the vite config. Not only is this tedious but VSCode extensions like Vitest also don't understand this extra file extension which hurts the DX quite a bit for writing runic code/tests.
(Yes, you need runes inside test files because you might test a module that receives some state)

### Describe the proposed solution

The solution would be that the compiler uses a more flexible matcher for compiling js/ts files, of the top of my head I came up with: `*.svelte.*{js,ts}`.
Here are a couple of test cases that showcase the matches:
```
svelte-module.ts // ignored
module-svelte.ts // ignored
svelte.module.ts // ignored
module.svelte.ts // match
module.svelte.test.ts // match
module.test.svelte.ts // match
```
This allows for more flexible file names that don't degrade the experience with testing. I'm sure there are more frameworks/libraries that also utilize file extensions (potentially storybook) so I wouldn't say this is an edge case but a pretty common use case.

A bonus would be if when checking the Vitest option through the CLI scaffolds these matchers.

### Importance

would make my life easier

title: Rename `$derived.call` to `$derived.lazy`
body:
### Describe the problem

In #10240 we added `$derived.call(fn)` alongside `$derived(expression)`, and somehow overlooked the fact that `Function.prototype.call` is a thing.

Strictly speaking this is fine — these are runes, not functions, and we can do what the hell we want. But realistically this is going to be a source of confusion at best and annoyance at worst for many people.

### Describe the proposed solution

Programmers often talk about 'lazy evaluation', which basically means providing a function to compute some value rather than the value itself.

Even though the under-the-hood mechanism of `$derived` is that it's _always_ lazy, meaning that this...

```js
let value = $derived(expression);
```

...is syntactic sugar for this...

```js
let value = $derived.call(() => expression);
```

...I think the conceptual framing is the right one. I therefore propose `$derived.lazy`:

```js
let a = $derived(expression); // evaluated eagerly
let b = $derived.lazy(() => expression); // evaluated lazily
```

We'll also need to add an error message for anyone who is already using `$derived.call`, of course.

### Importance

would make my life easier

title: Svelte 5: Allow more flexibility for `@render` tag expressions
body:
### Describe the problem

In React, if you have a `<Button>` component, you can spread its `children` into a `<button>` and it works fine.

```jsx
function Button({ foo, ...props }) {
    return <button {...props} />;
}
```

In Svelte, we have to do this:
```svelte
<script>
    let { children } = $props();
</script>

<button>
    {#if children}
        {@render children()}
    {/if}
</button>
```
It's quite boilerplate-y.

### Describe the proposed solution

Allow passing `children` to HTML elements.
```svelte
<script>
    let { children } = $props();
</script>

<button {children} />
```

### Alternatives considered

Just keep the current syntax, which is a tad bit boilerplate-y, but not a huge deal.

### Importance

nice to have

title: Debounced Binding
body:
### Describe the problem

While creating [this example REPL](https://svelte.dev/repl/6f543749f2f24e4fb28427dec562fd8a?version=4.2.0) about how to create a timer, I came to realize that directly binding an input field to the variable that triggers the start of the timer results in an immediate start of the timer.  But what if the user is not done typing?  Then the timer continuously restarts with every keystroke.

Not only does this look "bad" in a sense, but it is a performance hit.

So what's the usual option?  To debounce the `input` event, but oh oh!  I'm not handling the input event.  I am using value binding.  I have no place to debounce.

### Describe the proposed solution

It would be ideal if Svelte could provide debouncing on binding.  Something like this:

```html
<input type="number" bind:value|debounced={variable} /> <!-- default debounce time.  400ms? -->
<input type="number" bind:value|debounced={[variable, debounceTime]} />
```

In the example, `variable` is the bound variable, while `debouncedTime` is a variable containing the number of milliseconds to debounce the binding event.

### Alternatives considered

### Drop Binding

The obvious one:  Renounce the excellent Svelte feature and instead handle the `input` event in the "classic" way.

### Bind to another Variable.

In the example REPL, the bound variable is `countFrom`.  This is passed to the Timer component, which triggers the timer.  In order to debounce this, bind the input field to a new variable, and then use reactivity (`$:`) to start the debounce.  On timeout, the variable `countFrom` would be updated.

### Importance

would make my life easier

title: Should Svelte/SvelteKit expose which versions are running?
body:
### Context

Tools like Wappalyzer use heuristics to determine which technologies are used on a given page. Some of them can be a bit brittle. For example Svelte is [detected](https://github.com/wappalyzer/wappalyzer/blob/e0c0009302ec8880aa24217dd7281898a9833b40/src/technologies/s.json#L6665) via the `svelte-` CSS scoping classname prefix...

```js
"dom": "[class*='svelte-']"
```

...which only works for apps that use Svelte's built-in CSS scoping (rather than, say, Tailwind). This mechanism is also subject to change in future, at which point the heuristic will fail.

There's also no way to know which _version_ of Svelte (or SvelteKit) is running. This information is potentially useful (hypothetical use cases: devtools, tracking the speed of adoption of new versions, reaching out to sites that are running a version with a known vulnerability) and, in fact, the [CWV tech report](https://httparchive.org/reports/cwv-tech) plans to add version information to the report in future. Currently, Svelte is systematically underrepresented in reports of technology usage, and will be excluded altogether from these more granular reports.

The question under discussion here is whether Svelte and SvelteKit should expose information about whether they're being used on a given page, and if so, whether they should expose which versions are in use.

## Security and privacy

Of course, exposing version information provides potential attackers with information about which sites to target, if a version with a known vulnerability exists. Having said that, both client-side libraries and servers have been exposing version information for many years (see e.g. a default Apache 404 page, or log `_.VERSION` on any site running Underscore), and to my knowledge this isn't a practice that's frowned upon.

If we _do_ deem granular version information to be too sensitive, then there are alternatives (which might differ between Svelte and SvelteKit — for example we could provide major/minor/patch for Svelte but only major for SvelteKit):

- expose nothing
- expose a boolean ('this site is running some version of Svelte/SvelteKit')
- expose a major version ('this site is running Svelte 4 and SvelteKit 2')
- expose major/minor
- expose major/minor/patch

Crucially, an explicit mechanism (as opposed to a heuristic based on implementation details) can have an opt-out mechanism, so exposing the boolean is arguably _more_ privacy/security conscious than the status quo (and certainly not _less_).

For this to be at all useful, it would have to be opt-out rather than opt-in.

### Implementation

For Svelte, we could add something like this to an internal module...

```js
// svelte/internal/tracking.js
(window.__svelte_versions ??= []).push(VERSION);
```

...and then import that module in every compiled component (unless the compiler were configured to opt out):

```js
import 'svelte/internal/tracking';
```

For SvelteKit, it would be natural to use the `<meta name="generator">` tag, which is used by things like Wordpress:

```html
<meta name="generator" content="SvelteKit 1.20.0">
```

### Should we do this?

The consensus among maintainers was that exposing a boolean (with an opt-out) for both Svelte and SvelteKit would make sense, since it would simply be a more reliable and privacy-forward version of existing detection mechanisms. We're undecided about whether or not we should expose version information, however.

It's important to us that decisions like these happen with the community's consent and consultation, so we'd very much welcome your thoughts on this question.

*This post has been edited, so the first couple of replies might not make much sense*

### Describe the bug

The [solution](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/pull/7745) to the duplicate content `svelte:head` element [bug](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/6463) (and also [this one](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/6463)) requires HTML comments to be present in order to function correctly. Many [minification tools strip HTML comments](https://github.com/sveltejs/kit/issues/7493#issuecomment-1303218382), and as does CloudFlare by default in many environments.

Duplicating the `head` element is a fairly insidious bug because it isn't immediately obvious that anything is wrong, but for our project (in SvelteKit) it decreased performance by loading analytics scripts multiple times. body:
### Describe the problem

There are many cases where an application needs to connect DOM nodes with IDs:
* form fields and labels (`for`)
* accessible names (`aria-labelledby`)
* more [presented here](https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/111#discussioncomment-1517265)

Given that these IDs do not need any semantic meaning, and given that humans are pretty terrible at coming up with app-level unique IDs, this is a job wonderfully suited for a framework. Taking SSR into consideration, we cannot simply use counter-based solutions or randomly generated IDs.

### Describe the proposed solution

React 18 shipped its new [`useId()` hook](https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/111) which allows utilizing all the component tree knowledge of the framework and using that to generate IDs that are stable across SSR and unique across component instances.

I would like to see a similar thing in Svelte. It could look like this (`createInstanceId`):
```svelte
<!-- sign-in-form.svelte -->
<script lang="ts">
  import { createInstanceId } from 'svelte';
  
  const id = createInstanceId();
  const usernameID = `${id}-username`;
  const passwordID = `${id}-password`;
</script>

<label for={usernameID}>Username</label>
<input id={usernameID} />

<label for={passwordID}>Password</label>
<input id={passwordID} type="password" />
```

### Alternatives considered

#### Variable

The ID could come from a compiler-populated instance-specific variable:
```svelte
<label for={$$id}>Username</label>
<input id={$$id} />
```

Another name could be `$$instanceId`, to reflect its instance-dependency. This isn't perfect though, as it still doesn't communicate clearly enough that this isn't a component-specific variable, but rather an instance-specific one. A function call communicates that much better, similarly to `createEventDispatcher()`

#### Userland solution

I have used naive ID-generation solutions in the past (namely, [`lukeed/uid`](https://github.com/lukeed/uid)) and they didn't seem to cause any visible issues, but it's very likely that I simply haven't run into a use-case where a mismatch between the client and the server would be a problem.

Other userland solutions involve contexts, which is not great for developer experience, and might be problematic for asynchronous rendering (see https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/111#discussioncomment-1517189)

### Importance

would make my life easier

### Relevant mentions

https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/6932

title: Feature Suggestion: Improve versatility of `<svelte:component>` and `<svelte:element>` by treating them as a `<svelte:fragment>` when the `this` prop value is present but is a falsy or nullish value
body:
## Describe the problem

In some cases, I would like to conditionally render some content in a component or element.

## Describe the proposed solution

For these cases, it would be useful if we were able to conditionally omit the component or element by using a nullish or falsy value in the `this` prop. So this example (below) would simply render `Some text` since the `this` prop is a falsy value:

```svelte
<svelte:component this={false && MyComponent}>
  Some text
</svelte:component>
```

In such cases, the `<svelte:component>` or `<svelte:element>` would simply be treated as a `<svelte:fragment>`.

## Alternatives considered

The main alternative is see is similar but essentially creating my own `Fragment` component which simply returns the slotted content in this format:

```svelte
<slot {...$$restProps} />
```

In practice, it could be used like this:

```svelte
<svelte:component
  this={condition
    ? WrapperComponent
    : Fragment
  }
>
  Some text
</svelte:component>
```

The downside to this, aside from having to import another custom component is that it would not work at all for `<svelte:element>`. In those cases, I would actually have to create a Svelte component counterpart for every single element so I could use them against my new `Fragment` component like this:

```svelte
<script>
  import { Fragment, Div } from './customComponents.js';
  const condition = Math.random() < 0.5;
</script>

<svelte:component
  this={condition
    ? Div
    : Fragment
  }
>
  Some text
</svelte:component>
```

## Importance

would make my life easier

title: Add `envDir: false` option
body:
### Description

Currently, Dotenvx is not properly supported by Vite.

We are using [dotenvx](https://dotenvx.com/docs) (from the creator of dotenv) to manage our environment variables in Astro and Vite.
This means that a `.env` and a `.env.production` is available for every app in our monorepo with encrypted values, as follows:

SOME_ENV_VAR="encrypted:BA/01aCs2DHMHJc2SFeg...etcetc...f1TZg="

However, this currently results in Vite picking up the encrypted values without decrypting them. This results in unexpected situations, such as: running a production build with Astro as follows:
```bash
npx dotenvx run -f .env.production --strict -- astro build
```
I expect this command to only inject production .env values. However, Vite is automatically inserting the available `.env` file with encrypted values alongside the requested .env.production. This interferes with our Astro environment variable validation. We validate whether certain variables are present using Astro schema validation. Encrypted variables in the .env file are considered as "valid", even when encrypted (they are valid strings), therefore disrupting our env variable validation.

We currently use a workaround by setting the envDir to "bogus" in our Astro config. This is of course not a desirable solution.

Context @ Vite Discord: https://discord.com/channels/804011606160703521/1327200673518977046

Looking forward to work towards a solution together!

### Suggested solution

There are some directions:
- Adding an option to disable automatic .env-variable inclusion
- Adding a detection-mechanism for encrypted .env values
- ...

title: Add `module-sync` condition to default `ssr.resolve.externalCondition`
body:
### Description

[`module-sync` condition](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v22.10.0#new-module-sync-exports-condition) is a condition enabled by Node.js when `require(esm)` is enabled. It is supported by the config loader (https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/18650), but not by the SSR module loader.

### Suggested solution

Add `module-sync` condition to default `ssr.resolve.externalCondition`.

### Alternative

Leave it as-is and tell users to configure it when needed.

### Additional context

- related: https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/18300
- we don't support `export { foo as 'module.exports' }` (https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/54563) in the config loader but we should support that as well
- The reason of not proposing adding `module-sync` to `ssr.resolve.conditions` is to follow Node.js's recommendation.
  Quoting from the Node 22.10.0 release post:
  > For **bundlers/tools**: they should avoid implementing this stop-gap condition. Most existing bundlers implement the de-facto bundler standard [**`module`**](https://webpack.js.org/guides/package-exports/#providing-commonjs-and-esm-version-stateless) exports condition, and that should be enough to support users who want to bundle ESM from CJS consumers. Users who want both bundlers and Node.js to recognize the ESM exports can use both **`module`**/**`module-sync`** conditions during the transition period, and can drop **`module-sync`**+**`module`** when they no longer need to support older versions of Node.js. If tools do want to support this condition, it's recommended to make the resolution rules in the graph pointed by this condition match the Node.js native ESM rules to avoid divergence.

title: Re-export PostCSS config type from `postcss-load-config`
body:
### Description

As a developer using Vite I want to be able to write type-safe PostCSS configs using the same version of `postcss-load-config` Vite uses so that I do not accidentally write configs that Vite cannot load correctly.

### Suggested solution

In Vite, we could re-export the type `postcssrc.Config` from `postcss-load-config` so that developers can use that type to write type-safe PostCSS configs.

### Alternative

- Not vendor `postcss-load-config` code (as suggested in https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/15869#issuecomment-1939414914)
- Writing PostCSS config inside Vite config
  - This only accepts the array format, and many examples use the object format; converting from the object format to the array format is not the most straightforward, especially if plugin options are involved
  - On a more subjective note, I prefer having each tool's config in a separate file, as it helps me mentally separate the context I need to consider
- Adding a devDependency on `postcss-load-config` per project to get access to the type in each project using PostCSS
  - This requires that all projects using Vite keep track of the version of `postcss-load-config` used by Vite to not use a wrong version and accidentally write a wrong config
- Not writing type-safe configs

### Additional context

Now that Vite 6 has updated `postcss-load-config` to v6, developers can now load TypeScript PostCSS config files easily, but ensuring that these configs are type-safe require us to add an additional dependency on `postcss-load-config`, which is less than ideal due to the possibility of a project's `postcss-load-config` differing from Vite's, which can lead to hard to debug errors.

title: Support for SASS nodeJS package importer
body:
### Describe the bug

I am making a generic app that that offers both a SASS and a CSS stylesheet to users, so they can use whichever suits their needs. However, there is an issue with the import of node packages.

SASS now has the [--pkg-importer=node](https://sass-lang.com/documentation/cli/dart-sass/#pkg-importer-node) option that allows it to load dependencies using the Node.js module resolution algorithm. Using this CLI option i can import a path that is defined on the `package.json` "export".
```scss
@use "pkg:path/to/file.scss"
```

However, the above does not work in the context of a node app. With that, i mean that if we try to import the `.scss` containing the above code in a `main.js` file, we'll get:
> Error: Can't find stylesheet to import.

I checked the documentation but couldn't find a way to configure this or add the SASS importer as seen on the [sass example](https://sass-lang.com/documentation/js-api/interfaces/importer/).

I would expect that we can use the supported `pkg:` prefix to both build the SASS/SCSS file to css and serve a node app using that same code, or at least be able to configure the css options to enable that support.

Note: I understand that bootstrap does not have an "exports" property in their package.json. I used it for a simple example, the behavior is the same with packages that define "export".

### Reproduction

https://github.com/kkesidis/vite-sass-pkg-prefix

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `yarn build:scss`  to build the css file. This will succed.
2. Run `yarn build" to build the app (which also imports the scss file)

title: Update create-vite Vanilla and Vanilla TS to support CSP require-trusted-types-for
body:
### Description

The [Content Security Policy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy) (CSP) [`require-trusted-types-for`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/require-trusted-types-for) disallows direct `innerHTML` usage. Both the Vanilla JS and Vanilla TS starters use `innerHTML` to set up their app's initial HTML structure from `main.(js|ts)` and set the value of the counter when clicked from `counter.(js|ts)`. Because of this, both of these starters throw errors and don't work with this CSP in place.

While likely not a general problem for most Vite users, this does become a problem using these starters to test out [Isolated Web Apps](https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md), in-progress standards proposal. IWAs require this CSP as part of their runtime experience, so trying to spin up a quick sample app with either of these project bases causes immediate errors.

### Suggested solution

* For `coutner.(js|ts)`, replace the `innerHTML` with `textContent`. This works under that CSP and is the more appropriate property to be using
* For `main.(js|ts)`, either implement a sample `trustedTypes` policy (as shown in the MDN page above), update the code to use `createElement` calls and append them as needed, or write the HTML directly to `index.html` instead of injecting it through JavaScript

### Alternative

I'd considered suggesting adding an IWA starter, which may be useful down the line, but I don't think is needed right now, especially as these two changes will benefit everyone.

title: Export @vitejs/plugin-legacy options interface
body:
### Description

As a developer building a wrapper library around `@vitejs/plugin-legacy` ([nuxt-vite-legacy](https://www.npmjs.com/package/nuxt-vite-legacy)), I need to re-export the type `@vitejs/plugin-legacy` uses to accept user options, because I need to allow a user to configure `@vitejs/plugin-legacy` through `nuxt-vite-legacy`.

Currently, `@vitejs/plugin-legacy` only exports this:

```ts
export { cspHashes, viteLegacyPlugin as default, detectPolyfills };
```

I need it to also export `interface Options` from `packages/plugin-legacy/src/types.ts`:

https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/2687dbbd4e19c86f9888ee784c9b51598e8b79ca/packages/plugin-legacy/src/types.ts#L1-L5

Without that, I have to copy/paste the type into my project, which is not only sub-optimal but also plain wrong. My library supports `@vitejs/plugin-legacy@^4.0` (that is 4.0 and 4.1 at the moment), and the actual version may vary depending on user's project. If I copy/paste the options type from 4.1, this gives false expectations (advertise unsupported `renderModernChunks`) to users using 4.0, and if I copy/paste the type from 4.0, this will not expose `renderModernChunks` to users that have upgraded to 4.1.

### Suggested solution

In `packages/plugin-legacy/src/index.ts` we could do:

```ts
export type { Options } from "./types"
```


### Alternative

_No response_

### Additional context

If it were the application code, I could derive the type with:

```ts
import legacy from "@vitejs/plugin-legacy"
type Options = Exclude<Parameters<typeof legacy>[0], undefined>
```

However, that only works for the library itself, this doesn't allow to **re-export** the type for library users.

title: Use the Sass Compiler API
body:
### Description

We (the Sass team) have just released [a proposal](https://github.com/sass/sass/blob/main/proposal/shared-resources.d.ts.md) for a `Compiler` API in Sass that shares resources between different compilations (see also https://github.com/sass/sass/issues/3296). This is particularly useful when using the [`sass-embedded`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/sass-embedded) package, which runs a very fast subprocess to compile Sass: within the lifetime of a single `Compiler`, the subprocess will remain open, eliminating all the overhead of starting it and shutting it down that currently causes `sass-embedded` to be slower than it could be.

For now, we're just seeking your feedback on the proposal. Once it lands, we hope you'll integrate it into Vite for substantially improved performance.

### Suggested solution

Start a `Compiler` when Vite's build initializes and uses that compiler to compile all Sass files, so that Sass users using the embedded host experience better performance.

### Alternative

Runs a separate `sass.compile()` call for each compilation, which has a large amount of overhead when using sass-embedded.

title: Import paths with query parameters containing `../` cause path normalization to fail
body:
### Describe the bug

We're [@nuxtjs/i18n](https://github.com/nuxt-modules/i18n) running into an [issue](https://github.com/nuxt-modules/i18n/issues/2242) with the way paths are being normalized when the paths contain query parameters with (more than one) `../`. 

https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/df7799181c9e65a1557ca6ae7275962f00afd09d/packages/vite/src/node/utils.ts#L210

I understand that `path.posix.normalize` tries to make sense of the path containing `../`, but in our case it breaks the way files are being resolved later on. I noticed that the `rollup` plugin `@rollup/plugin-node-resolve` had [a similar issue](https://github.com/rollup/plugins/pull/487) and fixed it by splitting the query parameters before resolving a path. 

This is what is happening:
```
> path.posix.normalize('@nuxt/i18n/__config__?target=./config.ts')
'@nuxt/i18n/__config__?target=./config.ts'
> path.posix.normalize('@nuxt/i18n/__config__?target=../config.ts')
'@nuxt/i18n/__config__?target=../config.ts'
> path.posix.normalize('@nuxt/i18n/__config__?target=../../config.ts')
'@nuxt/i18n/config.ts'
> path.posix.normalize('@nuxt/i18n/__config__?target=../../../config.ts')
'@nuxt/config.ts'
```

I would think losing the query parameters or it influencing the path inside `normalizePath` is not intentional, but if it is, then do you have suggestions as to how to work around this? I would be happy to open a PR to implement a similar fix to the one referenced.

### Reproduction

### Steps to reproduce

Using imports with a query parameters containing more than one `../`, as seen in the reproduction, `import viteLogo from '/vite.svg?target=../../';` will fail to resolve.

title: Runtime-Conditional Dependencies for Published Packages
body:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

JavaScript packages can already select different code paths for different runtimes. Bun supports the `bun` conditional export alongside conditions such as `node`, `import`, `require`, and custom conditions. This lets a single published package expose a Bun-native implementation when executed by Bun and a portable fallback when executed by Node.js.

The dependency graph, however, cannot express the same distinction.

A package may need **no third-party dependency under Bun** because Bun provides a capability natively, while its Node.js fallback may require an additional package. Today the package author must usually choose between two undesirable outcomes:

1. declare the fallback package as a normal dependency, causing Bun consumers to install code they never use; or
2. make the fallback dependency optional/peer-based and force Node.js consumers to perform additional installation steps or discover a missing dependency at runtime.

The desired behavior is straightforward:

* a Bun consumer should install the package once and receive the minimal dependency graph required by the Bun implementation;
* a Node.js consumer should install the same package once and automatically receive the dependencies required by the Node.js implementation;
* consumers should not need runtime-specific package names or manual secondary install commands;
* package managers that do not understand any new Bun-specific metadata must remain correct, even if their install is less optimized.

This is not primarily an “optional dependency” problem. It is a mismatch between **conditional module resolution** and an **unconditional installation graph**.

Consider a library that provides one public API but has two internal implementations:

* **Bun:** uses a capability already built into Bun;
* **Node.js:** uses a third-party fallback package to provide equivalent behavior.

The library can already express the runtime-specific code selection through conditional exports. Bun explicitly documents the `bun` export condition and supports custom conditions as part of module resolution.

What the package cannot express is that the fallback dependency is required only by the Node.js branch.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[Published package] --> E[package.json exports]
    P --> D[package.json dependencies]

    E --> C{Runtime condition}
    C -->|Bun| B[Bun-native implementation]
    C -->|Node.js| N[Node-compatible fallback]

    B --> BN[Uses Bun-native capability]
    N --> NX[Requires fallback dependency X]

    D --> U[Dependency X installed unconditionally]
    U --> BI[Bun consumer installs X even though it is unused]
    U --> NI[Node consumer works automatically]

    BN --> GAP[Code selection is conditional]
    NX --> GAP
    BI --> GAP2[Dependency selection is not conditional]
    NI --> GAP2
```

The core mismatch is therefore:

> **The active runtime can change which implementation is loaded, but package metadata cannot correspondingly change which dependencies are required.**

This is increasingly relevant as runtimes provide more built-in capabilities and libraries attempt to expose a single portable API without penalizing users of richer runtimes.

The JavaScript ecosystem is no longer defined by a single server runtime with interchangeable package managers. Bun already has runtime awareness for module resolution; the missing piece is allowing that awareness to influence the package dependency graph safely and reproducibly.


### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Add support in Bun's package manager for **runtime-conditional dependency resolution for published packages**.

The feature should allow a package's **required dependency set to be a function of the target runtime**, just as the selected implementation can already be a function of runtime conditions.

The exact `package.json` syntax, configuration surface, and lockfile encoding are deliberately not prescribed here. Bu

title: Improve bun release signature infrastructure
body:
To support #39464 a revocation file and some pgp public keys should be committed to the repository.

The current signing key can be transitioned to the `Past` role, and epochs generated for all the previous releases before this new verification is deployed.

This has bun becoming its own verification tool for both previous and future releases and gives the maintainers a useful way to rotate keys.

An alternative would be to publish a separate rust binary for all supported platforms that would be more general purpose. It could eliminate dependence on OS provided checksum verification tools and accept a key fingerprint to serve as a root of trust along with a file to retrieve pgp keys from.

--------

## Release-Key Revocation Model

This design separates **authorization to publish current trust information** from **authorization to verify historical release artifacts**.

The checksum manifests remain separate signed files. The revocation response contains key and release-epoch information, but does not contain archive checksums.

### 1. Maintainer Options for Revocation

#### Embedded key roles

The client embeds three keys:

- **Past key** — used for older releases.
- **Current key** — used for the current release-signing period.
- **Future key** — used to prepare or authorize the next signing period.

Only the embedded current and future keys may sign the revocation response.

#### Revoking the past key

A revocation response signed by the current key may revoke past embedded keys only.

This allows maintainers to retire older keys while keeping the current key operational.

The current key may not:

- Revoke the future key.
- Revoke the current key (itself).
- Add new release keys.

#### Revoking the current key

A revocation response signed by the future key may revoke:

- Past embedded keys.
- The current embedded key.

This permits a transition from the current key to the future key.

The future key may not revoke itself.

#### Adding new release keys

Only a revocation response signed by the future key may provide new public keys.

A newly provided key can be added to the keyring for subsequent checksum-manifest verification, subject to the manifest’s revocation rules.

A new key may not be both provided and revoked in the same response.

#### Epoch-specific historical keys

An epoch can contain:

- A list of release names.
- One public key associated with those releases.

A release can belong to zero or one epoch.

If a release belongs to an epoch, the epoch’s key is included when verifying that release’s checksum manifest—even if that key has subsequently been revoked for future use.

This allows maintainers to revoke a signing key while preserving verification of immutable historical releases:

```text
Epoch 3 key:
    authorized for release v3.0.0
    later revoked for new releases
    still accepted for v3.0.0
```

A revoked epoch key is therefore not globally trusted. It is accepted only for the releases explicitly assigned to that epoch.

#### Releases without an epoch

If a release is not assigned to an epoch, its checksum manifest is verified using the unrevoked keys currently available in the revocation response:

- Unrevoked embedded keys.
- Unrevoked new keys.

### 2. What the Code Enforces

#### Revocation-response authentication

The revocation response must contain a valid cleartext PGP signature made by one of the embedded keys.

The signer’s role is then checked against the revocation policy:

- Past keys cannot sign revocation responses.
- Current keys may revoke past keys only.
- Future keys may revoke past or current keys.
- Future keys may not revoke themselves.

A response with no valid authorized signature is rejected.

#### Manifest version

The response must have:

```json
{
  "version": 1
}
```

Other versions are rejected. The version should be incremented and a different URL used when the schema is changed.

#### Revoked-key normalization

Revoked key IDs are trimmed and normalized to uppercas

title: bun build: emit bundled TypeScript declarations with path-alias rewriting (tsdown parity)
body:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

I am migrating a library from `tsdown 0.23.0` to `bun build` on `Bun 1.4.1+4661e494f`. The JS output is better overall. With 2 entrypoints, `target node`, `format esm`, `packages external`, `minify` and `splitting`, the bundle is fast and correct.

The blocker is types. `bun build` emits no `.d.ts` or `.d.mts`. The workaround `tsc --emitDeclarationOnly` preserves the `#/` alias in the emitted declarations, which breaks external consumers because `#/` only resolves inside the package via `package.json` `imports`. `tsdown` with `dts: true` emits a single bundled `.d.mts` chunk with aliases already resolved to relative paths.

Environment:
- `bun --revision`: `1.4.1+4661e494f`
- OS: `Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64`
- `node --version`: `v26.7.0`
- `typescript`: `7.0.2`
- previous bundler: `tsdown 0.23.0` with `entry: ["./src/index.ts", "./src/index.serverless.ts"]`, `minify: true`, `deps: { neverBundle: true }`

Verified minimal repro with 3 files in `src`, `package.json` with `imports` `#/*`, and `tsconfig` with `paths` `#/*`:

`package.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "bun-dts-repro",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "imports": {
    "#/*": "./src/*"
  },
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.mts",
      "import": "./dist/index.mjs"
    },
    "./extra": {
      "types": "./dist/extra.d.mts",
      "import": "./dist/extra.mjs"
    }
  }
}
```

`tsconfig.json`:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ESNext",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "paths": {
      "#/*": ["./src/*"]
    }
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}
```

`src/shared.ts`:

```ts
export const shared = 1;

export function formatShared(prefix: string) {
  return `${prefix}:${shared}`;
}
```

`src/index.ts`:

```ts
export { shared, formatShared } from "#/shared";
```

`src/extra.ts`:

```ts
export { formatShared } from "#/shared";
```

Steps:

```bash
bun install
bun build ./src/index.ts ./src/extra.ts --outdir ./dist --target node --format esm --packages external --minify --splitting --entry-naming "[name].mjs" --chunk-naming "chunk-[hash].mjs"
bun x tsc --emitDeclarationOnly --outDir dist --rootDir src
bun x tsc --noEmit -p consumer/tsconfig.json
```

`consumer/check.ts`:

```ts
import { shared } from "../dist/index.mjs";

console.log(shared);
```

Observed:
- JS bundles correctly to `index.mjs`, `extra.mjs` plus one shared `chunk-*.mjs`.
- No `.d.mts` is emitted by `bun build`.
- `tsc` emits `index.d.ts` still containing `from "#/shared"`.
- External check fails first with `TS7016` because exports expect `.d.mts` but only `.d.ts` exists:

```text
consumer/check.ts(1,24): error TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module '../dist/index.mjs'. '.../dist/index.mjs' implicitly has an 'any' type.
```

- After manually renaming `.d.ts` to `.d.mts`, the same check fails on the preserved alias:

```text
dist/index.d.mts(1,38): error TS2307: Cannot find module '#/shared' or its corresponding type declarations.
```

Related: #5141, which already tracks declaration emit and also mentions unresolved path aliases in `.d.ts`.

Impact: blocks migration. This prevents replacing `tsdown` with `bun build` for published libraries.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Add a `dts` option to `Bun.build` and a `--dts` / `--emit-dts` CLI flag, for example:

```ts
await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ["./src/index.ts", "./src/extra.ts"],
  outdir: "./dist",
  target: "node",
  format: "esm",
  packages: "external",
  minify: true,
  splitting: true,
  dts: true,
});
```

title: node:module.register / Node-internal ESM loader hooks are not implemented in Bun, breaking frameworks like Cordis
body:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

**Title:** `node:module.register` / Node-internal ESM loader hooks are not implemented in Bun, breaking frameworks like Cordis

**Body:**

## Summary

Bun implements most of the `node:module` API surface but does not implement the loader-hook machinery that Node exposes via `module.register()` and the internal `Module.registerHooks`-style synchronous hooks. Frameworks that depend on these hooks to drive **server-side hot module replacement** (HMR) — notably Cordis, which DeepSeek Harness uses for its profile boot pipeline — enter an infinite restart loop on Bun because the loader hook never signals module invalidation.

## Environment

- Bun: `1.4.0` (reproducible on `1.3.14+`)
- OS: macOS 22.6.0 (darwin x64)

## What breaks

Cordis' profile-boot flow contains a guard like:

```js
if (!signalShutdown.signal.aborted && ctx.fiber.state === 2 && ctx.get("loader") !== void 0) try {
  // run the loader hook to check for invalidation
  ...
}
```

Under Node this resolves once per change and exits. Under Bun `ctx.get("loader")` resolves to a working loader but Bun's implementation does not call the registered Node-compatible `Module.register` hooks, so the `loader` lookup never invalidates and the loop re-runs indefinitely (high CPU, eventual OOM).

A minimal repro would be a Cordis profile that uses `@cordisjs/loader` and any file change, but the upstream issue is more general: **anything relying on the Node ESM loader hook contract** (`module.register`, `Module.registerHooks`, or the `getFormat` / `resolve` / `load` synchronous hooks) does not work on Bun today.

## Why it matters

- HMR is a non-trivial UX feature for long-running dev servers (DSH itself, any Cordis-based app, various Vite-adjacent server tooling).
- The work-around the user is forced into is patching the framework's source to short-circuit the loop, which is fragile and version-coupled.

## Suggested fix

Implement the synchronous portion of `module.register` / loader hooks, at least:

- `module.register(specifier, parentURL, options)` returning a `MessagePort`-based hook channel.
- The `resolve`, `getFormat`, `getSource`, and `load` synchronous hook callbacks that Node documents at <https://nodejs.org/api/module.html#customization-hooks>.

This unlocks HMR and any other tooling that relies on the Node ESM customization-hook contract.

## References

- Node ESM customization hooks: <https://nodejs.org/api/module.html#customization-hooks>
- Node proposal: <https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/api/esm.md#moduleregisterspecifier-parenturl-options>
- Cordis loader (consumer affected): <https://github.com/cordis-lib/cordis>

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

> **Feature proposal:** Implement the synchronous half of Node's ESM customization-hook API on `node:module`:
>
> - `module.register(specifier, parentURL?, options?)` returning a `MessagePort` for hook communication.
> - Synchronous `resolve` / `getFormat` / `getSource` / `load` hook callbacks, matching <https://nodejs.org/api/module.html#customization-hooks>.
>
> This enables Node-compatible HMR pipelines (Cordis, etc.) under Bun without requiring every downstream framework to ship an in-place shim or disable HMR via an env-gated guard.

### What alternatives have you considered?

_No response_

The JavaScript ecosystem has an enormous collection of battle-tested Vite and Rollup plugins (such as `@vitejs/plugin-react`, `@vitejs/plugin-vue`, SVGR, MDX, PWA, and specialized asset/CSS transformers). 

Currently, migrating an existing frontend project or complex build pipeline to `Bun.build` / `Bun.serve` requires rewriting these plugins into Bun's native plugin format (`BunPlugin` with `setup`, `onResolve`, and `onLoad`). import { build } from "bun";

  outdir: "./dist",

    fromVitePlugin(vue()),
  ],
});

Proposed Hook Mapping
resolveId -> onResolve
load -> onLoad
transform -> onLoad (post-read transform pipe)
buildStart / configResolved -> setup initialization
Alternatives considered
Running Vite via bunx --bun vite, which works but sacrifices the native speed and simplicity of Bun.build and Bun.serve.
Manually rewriting plugins for Bun, which creates duplicate maintenance overhead and fragments the ecosystem.

Feature Request: Vite-compatible plugin mode / build hooks for seamless Vite project migration
body:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

Currently, migrating a project built with Vite to Bun (`Bun.build` or Bun's dev server) requires a complete rewrite of custom build plugins and environment setups. 

Vite's plugin ecosystem relies heavily on Rollup/Vite specific hooks (such as `transform`, `configureServer`, `buildStart`, `resolveId`, and `renderChunk`) and specific plugin options (`apply: 'build' | 'serve'`). Bun's plugin system currently only supports basic `onResolve` and `onLoad` lifecycle hooks.

Because of this gap:
1. Projects using popular Vite plugins (e.g., SVG transforms, custom asset handlers, framework-specific compilers) cannot easily port their build configuration to Bun.
2. Developers are forced to maintain separate bundler logic or remain tied to Vite/Node.js for production builds and development servers.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Introduce a Vite-compatible compatibility layer or extended build mode/hook system in Bun's bundler (`Bun.build`) and dev server.

Specifically:
1. **Build/Serve Mode Execution**: Allow plugins to run conditionally based on execution context (`mode: 'build' | 'serve'`).
2. **Extended Plugin Hooks**: Support Rollup/Vite-style plugin hooks (e.g., `transform`, `buildStart`, `generateBundle`) or provide an official adapter/compatibility wrapper (e.g., `@bun/vite-plugin-adapter`).
3. **Seamless Migration Path**: Enable `bun.config.ts` or `Bun.build()` to consume existing Vite plugins with minimal to no modification, making porting Vite applications to Bun straightforward and zero-friction.

### What alternatives have you considered?

1. Writing Custom Bun Plugins Manually: 
Re-implementing every existing Vite/Rollup plugin using Bun's native `onResolve` and `onLoad` hooks. This is time-consuming, hard to maintain across large projects, and creates duplicate effort for plugins already maintained by the community.

2. Running Vite on top of Bun runtime: 
Using Bun purely as a JS runtime (`bun run dev` or `bun run build` calling Vite). While this works, it misses out on Bun's ultra-fast native Rust/Zig-powered bundler (`Bun.build`) and native dev server performance gains.

3. Using SWC/Oxc/Rolldown wrappers: 
Relying on external transformer pipelines prior to feeding code into Bun, which adds complex build orchestration steps and unnecessary I/O overhead compared to native Bun plugin lifecycle support.

title: `http.Server` cannot adopt external sockets via `emit('connection')`
body:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

In latest bun canary there is massively improved support for `new tls.TLSSocket` which works great - thanks. This has almost unblocked our ability to run a node application on Bun, but there's one blocker remaining.

Node's `http.Server` has an internal `connectionListener` that attaches an
`HTTPParser` to every socket passed through the `connection` event. This
allows user code to feed arbitrary Duplex streams (e.g. a TLS-terminated
socket from a proxy) into `http.createServer()` by calling
`server.emit('connection', socket)`.

Bun's `http.Server` does not have a JS-side connection listener. HTTP
parsing is done natively by uWS, and uWS only parses sockets that the
server itself accepted via `listen()`. Calling `emit('connection', socket)`
registers no parser on the socket — `request` events never fire.

Here is a reproduction: 

[bun-repro-emit-connection.js](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30307977/bun-repro-emit-connection.js)


### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Bun's `http.Server` (in `_http_server.ts`) registers no JS-side listener
for the `connection` event. Connections are instead delivered via the
native `onServerConnection` callback — uWS calls this directly when a
TCP connection arrives on the listening socket. The internal HTTP parser
and response pipeline are wired to the native uWS handle, not to an
abstract Duplex interface.

In Node, `_http_server.js` does:

```js
this.on('connection', connectionListener);
```

Where `connectionListener` attaches an `HTTPParser` to the socket,
wires `socket.on('data', …)` → parser, and emits `request` when a
complete HTTP message is parsed. Any Duplex passed through the
`connection` event gets parsed.


### What alternatives have you considered?

A workaround is to listen the http.Server on an ephemeral loopback port and pipe the decrypted stream through a `net.connect()` bridge — an extra TCP connection per tunnel.

title: Proposal for Qwen 4: Context-Reset Multi-Agent Evaluation & Learn-From-Mistakes Pipeline
body:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

Current LLM evaluation and training pipelines suffer from context-dependent scoring illusions and static knowledge limitations. Models evaluated in shared-context multi-turn chats exhibit sycophancy, attention drift, and groupthink, leading to inflated benchmark scores that don’t reflect real-world robustness. Additionally, pretraining on internet-scraped data teaches what is but not what was wrong and how it was fixed. This results in models that are statistically competent but lack dynamic self-correction capabilities, causing failures in agentic/tool-use scenarios (e.g., Claude Opus 4.7 Adaptive scoring only 49 on Tool Use despite high overall benchmarks).

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

Implement a Context-Reset Multi-Agent Evaluation Pipeline combined with a Learn-From-Mistakes Training Data Integration:
Evaluation: Replace single-agent or shared-context multi-agent benchmarks with isolated agents that reset context per turn. Aggregate results via consensus/outlier detection to measure true robustness over context-dependent performance.
Training: Curate a high-signal dataset of production errors + verified fixes (not just raw web text). Use asymptotic error reduction signals from later training stages to distill the model’s true capability ceiling into the next version. Prioritize this error-fix data over generic internet scrapes for alignment and reasoning fine-tuning.
This shifts the paradigm from brute-force parameter scaling to intelligent, self-correcting iteration — mirroring expert cybersecurity practices where sandboxed testing and vulnerability remediation logs drive security more effectively than raw code volume.

### What alternatives have you considered?

Larger parameter counts / more internet data: Already proven inefficient; Qwen3.7 Max outperforms larger models like Claude Opus 4.7 via smarter architecture, not scale.
Shared-context multi-agent evaluation: Prone to groupthink and bias propagation; fails to isolate individual agent reasoning.
RLHF-only alignment: Optimizes for safety/compliance over functionality; leads to tool-use paralysis (e.g., Opus 4.7 Adaptive).
Static benchmark leaderboards: Measure test-taking ability, not real-world adaptability; no feedback loop to training.
None of these address the core issue: models need to learn from their own verified mistakes in an isolated, context-independent manner to achieve genuine robustness.

### What is the problem this feature would solve?

`Bun.hash.xxHash3` needs the entire input passed in at once, as a single buffer or string. That causes two problems with large files:

- You can't hash a file bigger than available RAM, since you can't hold the whole thing in memory to pass it in.
- Even when a file does fit, reading it fully into memory just to hash it spikes memory usage — wasteful when hashing many large files (e.g. media assets).

I want to hash large files on disk at xxHash3 speed, without loading each entire file into memory.

ASC MHL (Media Hash List), the standard manifest format for verifying media-file integrity across film and post-production, names XXH3 as an accepted hash algorithm. These manifests store an XXH3 value per file and later verify against it, and the files involved — camera footage, masters — are routinely larger than RAM. A streaming hasher that reproduces the canonical XXH3 value is what makes those large-file integrity workflows possible at all.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

A streaming/incremental xxHash3 hasher with the same shape as the existing `CryptoHasher`: create a hasher, call `.update(chunk)` repeatedly while reading the file in fixed-size chunks, then call `.digest()` for the final hash.

```js
const hasher = new Bun.hash.xxHash3Updated(); // exact name/entry point up to you
for await (const chunk of Bun.file("huge.mov").stream()) {
  hasher.update(chunk);
}
const hash = hasher.digest(); // === Bun.hash.xxHash3(wholeFile)
```

It would need to:

- Produce the exact same value as a one-shot `Bun.hash.xxHash3` over the full file, so streaming and one-shot are interchangeable.
- Stay SIMD-fast — no throughput regression versus the one-shot call.
- Hold only one chunk at a time, so memory stays constant regardless of file size, making files larger than RAM hashable.

### What alternatives have you considered?

- `CryptoHasher` already does `.update()`/`.digest()` streaming, but only for cryptographic hashes (sha256, etc.), which are far slower than xxHash3 — too slow for large-file throughput.
- Reading the whole file into memory and calling `Bun.hash.xxHash3` once: fails outright above RAM size, and is memory-heavy otherwise.
- Hashing each chunk separately and combining the results: changes the output, so it isn't a real xxHash3 of the file and can't match the one-shot value.

title: Bun.Image: add "hash" output mode to placeholder()
body:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

`Bun.Image#placeholder()` currently returns a `data:image/webp;base64,...` URL (~210 bytes). This is fine for a handful of images, but at scale — say, a feed with 50+ images — you're paying ~210 bytes × N in your HTML/JS payload just for blur placeholders.

The ThumbHash format itself is only 5–25 raw bytes (~28–36 base64 chars). For pages with many images it makes more sense to ship the ~800-byte ThumbHash decoder once and store one tiny hash per image.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

A `placeholder("hash")` overload that returns the raw ThumbHash as a `Uint8Array`:

```ts
const img = new Bun.Image(src);
const hash = await img.placeholder("hash"); // Uint8Array, 5–25 bytes
const base64 = Buffer.from(hash).toString("base64"); // ≤36 chars
```

The hash can then be decoded client-side with [evanw/thumbhash](https://github.com/evanw/thumbhash) (~800 bytes minified).

This would also clarify the existing API — `placeholder()` / `placeholder("dataurl")` continues to return a ready-to-use data URL, while `placeholder("hash")` gives the raw bytes for more advanced use cases.

### Type signature

```ts
interface Image {
  placeholder(as?: "dataurl"): Promise<string>;  // data:image/webp;base64,...
  placeholder(as: "hash"): Promise<Uint8Array>;  // raw ThumbHash bytes
}
```

### What alternatives have you considered?

- Computing the ThumbHash outside of Bun (e.g. pure-JS) — but this means decoding the full image in JS just to re-encode to a hash, which defeats the point of `Bun.Image`.
- Storing the data URL — works, but is ~8× larger than the hash per image.

title: feat: expose raw JavaScriptCore (JSC) code coverage data
body:
### What is the problem this feature would solve?

Currently, Bun has built-in code coverage support via `bun test --coverage`. However, the output is limited to predefined formats like Text, Lcov. 

In Node.js, developers can leverage the raw, low-overhead code coverage native to the V8 engine via `process.env.NODE_V8_COVERAGE` or the `v8.takeCoverage()` API. This raw data is crucial for monorepos, specialized enterprise toolchains, and building custom coverage reporters without relying on heavy source-instrumentation tools like `c8`, `monocart-coverage-reports`. Since Bun is powered by JavaScriptCore (JSC), we currently lack a similar way to extract the raw bytecode-level execution data that JSC natively tracks internally.


### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?


We would like Bun to provide parity with Node.js's V8 coverage capabilities by exposing JSC's native coverage data, either programmatically or via environment variables.
## 1, Programmatic API (Mirroring Node's v8 module)
```js
// Proposed API in Bun (equivalent to Node's v8.takeCoverage())
import { jsc } from "bun"; // or via a new/existing internal module

jsc.startCoverage();
// ... execute code / tests ...
const rawJscData = jsc.takeCoverage(); // Returns raw JSC bytecode/block execution map
jsc.stopCoverage();
```
## 2, Environment Variable
An env var like `BUN_JSC_COVERAGE=./dir`, mirroring Node's `NODE_V8_COVERAGE`, which dumps raw JSC coverage JSON profiles to a specified directory upon process exit.

### Additional context
Just as Node.js exports raw coverage data in the native V8 coverage format, Bun should ideally export data in the native JSC coverage format.

JavaScriptCore already features a highly optimized internal tracking system via its Type Profiler and Code Coverage Profiler at the LLInt and Baseline JIT layers. Bun does not need to convert this to standard V8 or Lcov formats internally for this API; simply dumping JSC's native raw JSON/structural execution maps directly to the user would be enough. The community and custom tooling builders can then handle the parsing or conversion to third-party formats. This ensures maximum execution performance while granting full flexibility for advanced test engineering workflows.

### What alternatives have you considered?

_No response_

title: Tools CLI: resolve multiple matching instances by recency and add a --port target-selection flag
body:
## Problem Statement

When two (or more) `storybook dev` processes serve the same project — same config dir, different ports, possibly different process cwds — the `storybook tools` CLI cannot attach to any of them. It even prints the URL of the newest instance ("Found your Storybook running at http://localhost:6007") and then exits 1 because multiple registry records match. The suggested remediation (`--config-dir`) cannot disambiguate, because both instances share the same config dir, and there is no `--port` flag on `storybook tools` (`error: unknown option '--port'`).

This is a regression in behavior relative to the older `storybook ai` passthrough, which in the same situation selects the most recently started matching instance, sends the call, and prints a warning listing the competing instances with guidance on how to target another one (including a `-p, --port` flag).

Agents hit this in practice: a preview-launched Storybook plus a manually started one, or a stale-but-alive instance from an earlier session, is enough to make every runtime tools command hard-fail.

## Solution

Bring the tools attach path up to parity with the instance-selection behavior the shared resolver already implements (and the `storybook ai` CLI already uses):

1. **Recency selection on multiple matches.** When several running instances match the target project, attach to the winner the shared resolver picks (agent-bucket preference, then most recently started, pid tie-break) instead of hard-failing. This applies to `auto` and `--attach` alike.
2. **Sibling warning.** When siblings competed, surface a warning naming the chosen instance and the competing ones (url, cwd, config dir), and how to target a different one with `--port`. The warning must not corrupt `--json` output.
3. **`-p, --port` target-selection flag** on the `storybook tools` CLI and a matching `port` option in the `createTools` SDK, constraining instance matching to that port. When the project matches but no instance runs on the given port, fail with a port-mismatch message listing the running instances and their ports.
4. **Fix the remediation text.** Multi-instance guidance must suggest a disambiguator that actually works (`--port`), never a `--config-dir` value both instances share.

After the fix, in the two-instance repro: `npx storybook tools stories preview ...` from the project exits 0, uses the newest instance's port, and prints the sibling warning.

## User Stories

1. As an agent using the tools CLI, I want runtime commands to succeed when multiple Storybooks serve my project, so that a second running instance doesn't hard-fail every command.
2. As an agent using the tools CLI, I want the CLI to attach to the most recently started matching instance, so that the instance I (or the user) just launched is the one that answers.
3. As an agent that launched a Storybook via a preview tool, I want instances launched by my own agent to be preferred over others, so that my calls land on the Storybook I control.
4. As an agent using the tools CLI, I want a warning listing the competing instances whenever more than one matched, so that I can tell the user and pick a specific one if results look wrong.
5. As an agent using the tools CLI, I want a `--port` flag, so that I can address one specific instance when several share the same cwd and config dir.
6. As an agent passing `--port` with a port where no matching instance runs, I want an error listing the matching instances and their actual ports, so that I can correct the port without re-discovering state myself.
7. As an agent using `--attach` (hard-require attach), I want multiple matches to resolve by recency rather than error, so that strict attach mode is still usable on machines with several running Storybooks.
8. As an SDK consumer of `createTools`, I want a `port` option with the same semantics as the CLI flag, so that programmatic callers can target one instance deterministically.
9. As an SDK consumer, I want the attach

title: Tools CLI: proxy `review create` over the dev server's MCP endpoint and take ownership of the shared ai-CLI modules
body:
Part of the M5a tools CLI work ([#35724](https://github.com/storybookjs/storybook/issues/35724), PR [#35719](https://github.com/storybookjs/storybook/pull/35719)). This spec covers the final gap in that PR's tool surface, agreed in review discussion (proposal v12).

## Problem Statement

`storybook tools review create` is the one tool in the new `storybook tools` CLI that cannot work: creating a review requires the running dev server's review service, and the tools CLI runs fully disconnected. Connect mode (Milestone 5b) would solve this properly, but it may not land in time — meanwhile the CLI surface must be complete so the legacy `npx storybook ai <tool>` passthrough can later be deprecated.

Separately, the tools CLI leans on modules owned by that same legacy ai CLI (instance discovery, config-dir resolution, schema help rendering). Building the review proxy on top of them would deepen a dependency on code slated for removal.

## Solution

Two clearly separated commits on PR #35719:

1. **Relocation (refactor, behavior-neutral).** The modules both CLIs need — and that must outlive `storybook ai` — move out of the ai CLI's tree into the tools CLI's tree. The ai CLI imports them from there for its remaining lifetime, so its eventual removal becomes a pure deletion of its directory plus its two registration lines.
2. **Review proxy (feature).** The tools CLI proxies `review create` to the running dev server's MCP endpoint (the `display-review` tool) — the same mechanism the ai CLI passthrough uses — as an explicit stopgap until Milestone 5b connect mode. The proxy lives in the CLI dispatch layer; toolset definitions stay consumer-agnostic.

## User Stories

1. As an agent using the tools CLI, I want `storybook tools review create` to create a review in the running Storybook, so that the entire toolset surface works from the CLI without any MCP client setup.
2. As an agent, I want my review arguments validated locally against the toolset schema before any network call, so that bad input fails fast with the same error shape as every other tool.
3. As an agent invoking `review create` with no dev server running, I want the uniform "start the dev server first" contract, so that recovery is obvious.
4. As an agent invoking `review create` against a dev server without a ready MCP endpoint, I want explicit guidance to install/enable `@storybook/addon-mcp`, so that I can self-recover without reading source.
5. As an agent, I want `--json` to print the proxied reply's structured content, so that scripted consumers get machine-readable output.
6. As an agent, I want the exit code to reflect the proxied reply's error flag, so that shell pipelines behave correctly.
7. As an agent, I want `tools review create --help` rendered from the local toolset definition, so that help works with no dev server running.

9. As a Storybook user with review gated to trusted local clients, I want the CLI's requests to carry the trusted-local-client marker, so that review is enabled per-request just as it is for the ai CLI passthrough.
10. As a user of `npx storybook ai <tool>`, I want its behavior unchanged by the relocation, so that the refactor is invisible until the deprecation actually ships.
11. As a maintainer, I want zero imports from the tools CLI into the ai CLI's tree, so that dependency direction is dying-code-depends-on-living-code only.
12. As a maintainer, I want the future `storybook ai` removal to be a pure deletion (its directory plus its registration lines), so that the deprecation PR is trivially reviewable.

title: CLI: Run `storybook tools test run` without a dev server
body:
Follow-up to #35716 (Milestone 5a, PR #35719). Lands in PR #35719 itself per the agreed scope.

## Problem Statement

The `storybook tools` CLI runs Storybook's agent toolsets in a standalone process, fully disconnected from a dev server: docs and module-graph tools already work locally. `test run` — the tool that runs story tests via `@storybook/addon-vitest` — is the exception: it is marked `requiresDevServer` and the CLI refuses it, telling the user to start Storybook first. That requirement is incidental, not essential: the vitest child process that actually runs the tests is fully headless (it builds its own IPC channel, prepares its own stores, and boots vitest with its own Vite servers). The only dev-server-bound piece is the *responder* — the listener that answers a test-run request over the channel — which is wired exclusively in the dev server's `experimental_serverChannel` hook.

## Solution

Wire the test-run request listener from addon-vitest's `services` preset hook — the same hook that registers the `test` toolset — so every consumer that can offer the tool can also answer it, with the expensive machinery (story index for the store's initial state, leader store, vitest child boot) created lazily on first request. The dev server keeps its eager store creation (the manager UI needs it) through the same memoized ensure function, so its behavior is unchanged. With the responder available in-process, the `requiresDevServer` trait comes off `test.run` and the CLI's existing generic local path runs story tests end to end: `npx storybook tools test run` works in a project with no Storybook running, prints the same markdown report the MCP tool produces, and exits with a code reflecting the run outcome.

## User Stories

1. As a coding agent, I want `storybook tools test run` to work without a running Storybook, so that I can verify UI changes from a plain shell without booting a dev server.
2. As a coding agent, I want focused runs via story selectors (`--stories`), so that I get fast feedback on just the stories I am editing.
3. As a coding agent, I want to omit selectors to run all story tests, so that I can do full-project verification before finishing a task.
4. As a coding agent, I want the a11y toggle (`--a11y false`) honored locally, so that I can skip accessibility checks when I only need component results.
5. As a coding agent, I want the CLI report to match the MCP tool's markdown report, so that my parsing and habits transfer between the two surfaces.
6. As a coding agent, I want `--json` to emit the structured run result, so that I can consume statuses programmatically.
7. As a coding agent, I want the exit code to reflect the outcome (failure/cancelled runs exit non-zero), so that scripts and CI steps can gate on it.
8. As a coding agent, I want story-selector misses reported per selector (and a partial match to fail rather than silently run a subset), so that I never mistake a partial run for a full verdict.
9. As a coding agent, I want the CLI process to exit promptly once the result is printed, so that the command does not hang on lingering child-process handles.
10. As a coding agent, I want `--cwd` and `--config-dir` respected for test runs like every other tools command, so that I can run from anywhere.
11. As a coding agent, I want `storybook tools --help` to show `test run` as local instead of "requires running Storybook", so that discovery reflects reality.
12. As a developer using the Storybook UI, I want the test panel and watch mode to behave exactly as before, so that this change is invisible in the dev server.
13. As an MCP client user, I want `run-story-tests` behavior unchanged, so that existing agent integrations keep working.
14. As a developer running static builds, `storybook index`, or `storybook ai` metadata generation, I want no test machinery booted in those contexts, so that they stay fast and side-effect free.

body:
Milestone 5a of the Storybook Skills workstream (#35526), rescoped on 2026-07-31: deliver the public `storybook tools` CLI, derived at runtime from the shared OSA core toolsets, running the OSA in the CLI's **own process** — fully disconnected from the dev server. Stacks on Milestone 4 (#35677); the dev-server-connected mode ("attach") is Milestone 5b and out of scope here.

## Problem Statement

Coding agents working with Storybook can only reach the core toolsets (`docs`, `stories`, `test`, `review`) through MCP — either `@storybook/addon-mcp` on a running dev server or the hosted `@storybook/mcp`. There is no way to invoke these capabilities from a plain shell command, even though the capabilities themselves (Milestones 2 and 4) were built as consumer-agnostic toolset definitions, and even though the toolset descriptions already cross-reference a CLI spelling (`npx storybook tools stories changed`) that does not exist yet. Skills-based agent workflows — the primary direction of the workstream — need a CLI surface that requires no MCP client configuration and no running dev server for the capabilities that don't inherently need one.

## Solution

A public, unflagged `storybook tools` command that is a **pure consumer** of the toolset registry:

- It loads the target project's Storybook configuration (which already runs every `services` preset hook, registering all services and toolsets in the CLI's own process) and derives its entire command surface from the registered toolsets at runtime — `storybook tools <toolset> <kebab-cased-method>`, the exact spelling the toolset descriptions already freeze.
- Handlers are invoked unchanged with a CLI consumer context; their `ToolsetOutcome` maps mechanically to the terminal: markdown to stdout, `--json` prints the structured data, `ok` drives the exit code.
- Documentation commands work with no dev server at all. Commands that require a running dev server are marked with a `requiresDevServer` trait on their method definitions and present one uniform contract: "start the dev server first." `stories preview` runs as soon as a running instance is discovered (via the runtime instance registry the dev server already writes); state-bound commands report plainly that attaching is not yet available.
- The module graph is hosted in the CLI process cleanly (no logic changes): builder-vite implements its already-declared change-detection-adapter interface for the headless case, and the CLI repeats the dev server's own bootstrap sequence — making `stories changed` and `stories find-by-component` work locally on Vite projects.
- The top-level `--help` is the complete agent discovery surface: every tool with its full CLI-vocabulary description, input schema, and output schema (where declared) in a single dump.

1. As a coding agent, I want `npx storybook tools --help` (or bare `npx storybook tools`) to print every tool the target project provides — full descriptions, input schemas, and declared output schemas — so that I can learn the entire surface in one invocation instead of paying a multi-second project load per lookup.

title: Skills M4: addon-mcp and @storybook/mcp run on the shared core toolsets
body:
Part of the Storybook Skills workstream — see the tracking issue #35526 (Milestone 4). Builds on the public toolset layer from #35516 (Milestone 2); the work is stacked on that PR's branch and retargets to `next` when it merges.

## Problem Statement

Storybook exposes agent capabilities through two MCP surfaces — `@storybook/addon-mcp` (dev-server MCP at `/mcp`) and `@storybook/mcp` (hosted/static manifests) — and soon a CLI (`npx storybook tools`, Milestone 5). Today every addon-mcp tool body carries its own implementation (story-index reads, git/status logic, manifest access, formatting, telemetry), and `@storybook/mcp` duplicates the docs formatting logic that Milestone 2 ported into core. Every improvement to a tool's behavior, description, or output must be made two or three times, and the copies drift — Milestone 2's parity port only froze the drift, it didn't remove the duplication.

## Solution

Both MCP packages become thin adapters over the shared core toolsets (`docs`, `stories`, `test`, `review`) defined with `defineToolset`. Each package keeps only its frozen public contract (tool names, schemas, endpoint) and its transport; data, descriptions, formatting, and telemetry move into the toolset definitions, written once and consumed by addon-mcp, `@storybook/mcp`, and (in Milestone 5) the CLI. **The public MCP contract does not change: no tool renames, no schema changes, no endpoint changes, byte-identical output.**

## User Stories

1. As an agent connected to a dev-server MCP, I want the existing nine tools to keep their exact names, schemas, descriptions, and output, so that my workflows and any automation built on the endpoint keep working unchanged.
2. As an agent, I want tool responses to carry both the text I read and the `structuredContent` matching the published `outputSchema`, so that MCP Apps (the preview-stories carousel) and programmatic clients keep functioning.
3. As a user of a hosted Storybook MCP (Chromatic per-build or self-hosted), I want the `@storybook/mcp` docs tools to keep their public API and output, so that nothing observable changes for me.
4. As a Storybook maintainer, I want each capability's behavior, agent-facing prose, and formatting defined once in a toolset, so that improvements land on every surface at once instead of drifting across copies.
5. As a Storybook maintainer, I want the eval-tuned MCP descriptions to become the canonical toolset descriptions, so that the Milestone 5 CLI inherits proven prose for free.
6. As a maintainer, I want descriptions to cross-reference sibling tools in each consumer's vocabulary (MCP tool names vs CLI commands), so that agents are never told to call a tool that doesn't exist on their surface.

9. As a user of Storybook composition (refs), I want multi-source docs listing to keep working with per-source failure isolation, so that one broken source doesn't take down documentation for the rest.
10. As a user on an unsupported builder, I want `get-stories-by-component` to tell me the module graph is booting/unavailable/failed rather than claiming every component has no stories, so that I don't draw wrong conclusions.
